extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Doctrinal rules and standards governing the creation, assignment, forfeiture, implied scope, remedies, and antitrust limits of licenses under patent law. Covers express and implied licenses, assignability, estoppel, shop-rights, remedies, and interaction with the Sherman Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of subsequent agreement on license
rubrics_metrics.description: A termination of a license by a new agreement will end or will modify the relation of the parties to the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties enter a new agreement, the new instrument controls the parties' relations with respect to the licensed rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner's right to sue licensee for infringement limited by termination/forfeiture
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the license does not contain a forfeiture clause the owner may sue his licensee for infringement only on a showing that the license has terminated by mutual consent or that it has been forfeited by decree of a court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The owner may not, in an infringement suit involving such a license, prove in that suit the fact of a breach that would entitle him to forfeiture; forfeiture must be established in a direct proceeding (equity) unless the license itself contains a forfeiture clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies when license genuinely forfeited and licensee continues
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a license is really forfeited, and the licensee continues to work under it as though it were still in force, the licensor has an option to sue him as an infringer, or to sue him for the promised royalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the licensor sues as an infringer, the act is regarded as repudiation of the license and the license is at an end; the alleged infringer may interpose any defence he could have had absent the license. Exceptions include situations where the licensee holds forth to the public by marking articles as manufactured under the patent, and where the licensee covenanted not to contest validity (estoppel for life of patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of action for recovery of royalties
rubrics_metrics.description: If the licensor selects to sue for the promised royalties, he must sue at law; except where he sues an assignee of the licensee for royalties accruing before the assignment, in which case the action for their recovery must be brought in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of remedies affects available defenses and doctrines (e.g., prior art evidence may be introduced in a royalties suit to construe the patent and ascertain royalty-bearing acts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of prior art in royalty suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever the licensor sues for the promised royalties, the defendant may introduce evidence of the prior art, to guide the court to the construction of the patent, and thus to aid in the ascertainment of the extent of those doings of the licensee which are subject to the payment of royalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art evidence helps define the scope of the patent and therefore what conduct triggers royalty obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture may disentitle use of license-granted trade-names
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a license to make and sell patented articles conferred also a right to designate those articles by an arbitrary identifying name, a forfeiture of the license will disentitle the licensee to use that name to designate competing articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forfeiture can reach ancillary license privileges such as exclusive use of trade-designations granted by the license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignability requires express or clearly implied words
rubrics_metrics.description: No license is assignable by the licensee to another, unless it contains words which show that it was intended to be assignable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most suitable phrase is 'assigns'; words like 'legal representatives' have been held to suffice in some cases; extrinsic facts and conduct may also indicate intent to permit assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic facts and conduct can render a license assignable
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic facts and circumstances and the conduct of the parties may give an assignable character to a license which on its face is not assignable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may look beyond the written phraseology to the parties' behavior and surrounding circumstances to determine assignability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successor entities and receivers may invoke licenses in certain situations
rubrics_metrics.description: A consolidated railroad company may invoke licenses given to constituent corporations because the consolidated company is a successor rather than an assignee; likewise a receiver authorized to manage corporate business may be protected by a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successor status (e.g., consolidation) or a receiver appointed to operate a corporation can inherit or invoke the license; by contrast, a receiver appointed in supplementary proceedings to settle an individual's business does not acquire rights to an unassignable license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of partnership dissolution on partnership license
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a license is given to a partnership and that partnership is dissolved, if the business is continued by one of the partners that partner is entitled to that license; but where such a dissolution ends the business of the partnership, the license lapses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A receiver appointed to wind up partnership affairs may invoke the license to protect him in winding up; context matters (continuation vs. termination of business).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited scope of a license to one person
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to one person gives no right to any partner of that person, or to any corporation organized by the licensee; although the licensee may employ agents to manufacture the patented article for him; and if it authorizes the licensee to act only at a particular place, it will not protect any of his doings elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licenses are construed according to the natural import of their terms; personal and territorial limitations are enforced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-assignability may be waived by licensor
rubrics_metrics.description: The non-assignability of a license may be waived by the licensor; and will be so waived if he accepts the promised royalty from the assignee of the license, or ratifies the transfer by otherwise treating the assignee as the licensee was entitled to be treated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance of performance from an assignee or conduct treating an assignee as licensee can estop the licensor from asserting non-assignability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservation of personal operating right can limit assignor's sublicensing
rubrics_metrics.description: A reservation in an assignment, reserving the right to the assignor to operate fully under the patent but restricting the right to him personally will prevent the assignor from authorizing a third party to operate under the license when the assignor has no interest in the business other than a reservation of a royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reservations that purport to give the assignor only a personal right are construed to prevent delegation or authorization to third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignable licenses must be assigned whole unless partial assignment expressly allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignable licenses are assignable only in their entirety; unless they expressly or impliedly authorize their assignment in parts, and to a plurality of persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial assignments require explicit or clearly implied authorization in the license agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalties payable to licensor are assignable and follow the license with notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The royalties payable to a licensor are assignable by him; and the assignee's rights to those royalties follow the license, when it is assigned to a person who has notice of those rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice to the licensee regarding assignment of royalties is important to establish assignee's entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchaser of a license takes it subject to its restrictions and liabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The purchaser of a license takes it subject to all the restrictions connected therewith, whether he has notice of those restrictions or not; and is subject to liability for the same rate of royalty for his doings as the original licensee would have been.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buyers succeed to both benefits and burdens of the license as written, notwithstanding actual notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied licenses arise from acquiescence or estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Implied licenses, from conduct of owners of patent rights, may arise out of a considerable number of classes of facts; but, when analyzed, those facts will probably always be found to operate by virtue of the doctrines of acquiescence or estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a patentee joining a partnership passes an implied license to the partnership; patentee's acquiescence in use with acceptance of partial compensation implies a license unless other facts negate it; payment of full compensation is a convincing ground for an implied license. No implied license from acquiescence unless licensor had knowledge of the thing acquiesced in; omission to act must not be otherwise explainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel-implied license from inducing or concealing infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the owner explains the patented invention to a person ignorant of the patent and advises him to make/use/sell it with intent to induce infringement, and that person incurs expense in infringing or preparing to infringe, an implied license results by estoppel; similarly where the owner conceals the patent to allow infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misleading or concealing conduct by the patentee that induces expense or reliance gives rise to an implied license by estoppel to the misled party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of patented machine by one without patent interest can estop later suit
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a person sells a patented machine to another without having any interest in or under the patent, he will be estopped from prosecuting his vendee for infringement on the basis of any after-acquired title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That estoppel extends only to machines made or sold by permission or with the co-operation of the person acquiring title; does not necessarily protect post-dissolution acts by former partners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seller of a patent that infringes a prior patent is estopped from suing grantee
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a person sells a patent which employs an invention which infringes a prior patent, the person selling is estopped from bringing an action against his grantee for that infringement, even though the earlier patent is acquired after the sale of the later patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That estoppel operates as a license against the seller and owners in common with him of the prior patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor selling specimen without notice of forthcoming patent application is estopped
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an inventor before applying for a patent sells a specimen of his invention to a manufacturer who avowedly buys it to copy, and where the seller gives the buyer no notice of intent to apply for a patent, the inventor is estopped from bringing an action on such a patent against anyone for using or selling a specimen made by that purchaser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sale to a party who copies, without notice, can preclude later enforcement of the patent as to that specimen and users of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of a component part does not imply license to use combination
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to use a patented device may not be implied from the fact that the patentee has sold to the alleged infringer an article which constitutes one element of the patented combination, where the article is capable of other uses, even though usually sold as part of the complete patented device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts distinguish sale of multipurpose components from sale of a complete patented article when determining implied licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shop-right (employer's implied license for employee inventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an employee, during employment, conceives an invention applicable to employer's business, uses employer's property reducing it to practice, and the employer thereafter makes/uses/sells specimens without demanding present or prospective compensation, an implied license or 'shop right' results to the employer under any patent that may be granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shop-rights cover specimens the employer may make/use/sell during the life of the patent or may be confined to specimens made/used/sold with the inventor's knowledge during employment depending on equities; benefit may pass to assigns or successors depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery of full royalty or profits can operate as implied license in limited ways
rubrics_metrics.description: An actual recovery of a full royalty for making and selling to others operates as an implied license to any purchaser of the thing thus made and sold to use it to the same extent that he could lawfully have done if the maker had been licensed to make and sell it. But a recovery of mere nominal damages does not operate as an implied license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recovery of both damages and profits from a manufacturer may bar further suits by the patentee against users of specific articles covered by the decree, but recoveries are confined to use occurring before suit (if at law) or before final decree (if in equity); such recoveries do not license continuation or new use thereafter. Also, a decree for profits against a manufacturer does not necessarily constitute a defense to a suit against a user in all circumstances; details turn on the form of the recovery and decree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on license restrictions under Sherman Antitrust Act
rubrics_metrics.description: While courts long held that the owner of a patent has 'absolute freedom' in the use or sale of rights under the patent and may impose conditions on assignees/licensees (including price conditions) that are not in their very nature illegal, questions arise about the extent to which the Sherman Anti-Trust Act circumscribes such monopoly powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bement v. National Harrow upheld reasonable conditions (including fixed-price clauses) as not contrary to the Sherman Act; Henry v. Dick (split decision) and later decisions (e.g., Standard Sanitary) show limits—schemes by patentees and licensees to control prices, eliminate 'seconds' or otherwise combine to restrain trade may be subject to Sherman Act prosecution. The inquiry examines the substance and effect of the licensing scheme (e.g., concerted price control among many licensees) rather than formalistic label.
